2.3 SUMMARY IN ENGLISH Upon consideration by the Norwegian Go vernment, a Committee was appointed in Fe bruary 1990 to review the current Act on Con trol ofPrices, Profits and Restraints ofCompe tition of 26 June 1953, with the aim to propose new legislation in this field. The Committee has been chaired by Mr. A.C. Stray Ryssdal, with Mr. Egil Bakke, Ms. Jorunn Berland, Mr. Juul Bjerke, Ms. Else Bugge Fougner, Mr. Ei nar Hope and Ms. Tone Of stad as members. On 1 October 1991 the Committee handed down its report - «Competition for Economic Efficiency». The Committee proposes two separate statu tes to replace current legislation - a general Competition Act; and a Special Act vesting le gal authority with the Government to esta blish temporary price controls, but only provi ded that the risk of extraordinary inflationa ry or deflationary pressure is imminent. The main part of the Committee's report spells out the details of the proposalfor the ge neral Competition Act, - i.a. on substantive rules, the supervising authorities, rules on en forcement and sanctions, and on provisions enabling Norwegian authorities to assist for eign and supranational competition agenci es. The Committee submits that the established regulatory purpose of the Competition Act should be to promote economic efficiency. It is acknowledged that it may be difficult to deter mine in practice whether resources are in f act being put to their most efficient use. But since the analytical criteria are welldefined, econo mic efficiency as a designated purpose may be promoted through focused and vigorous ef forts on the part of the supervising authorities. When the center ofattention is on economic ef ficiency the risk that enforcement efforts may get sidetracked or become counterproductive because of internally con flicting regulatory goals is eliminated. More over, workable competition becomes the cen tral remedy under such a regime. The structu re of competition pressure in the various mar kets shall constitute the field under regulatory scrutiny. If workable competition is attained, pre vious monopoly profits are redistributedfrom monopolies and cartels to consumers, and the public welfare is subsequently increased. Un der the Committee's proposal, the guiding principle for supervision and enforcement ef forts shall be to break market power in order to effect this kind of redistribution. The Com mittee maintains however that the Competi tion Act and the competition authorities are unfit to promote any other forms of redistribu tion - benefitting e.g.

this kind of redistribution. The Com mittee maintains however that the Competi tion Act and the competition authorities are unfit to promote any other forms of redistribu tion - benefitting e.g.
specific districts, groups or trades. To what extent special interests are to be enhanced over the public good is a mat ter ofpolitical choice. Accordingly, the choice should be made by political bodies (the Parlia ment and the Government) directly answera ble to the electorate. Any attempt to let the Competition Act advance such deviating goals constitutes an implicit delegation of po litical authority that a competition agency would not be fit to exercise. Such delegation would also run counter to constitutional prin ciplesfor allocation of power. The Committee's recommendations are in fluenced by the contents and design ofsimilar statutory instruments in other countries with efficient competition legislation, as well as by European Community law. The Committee has kept in touch with corresponding commit tees in Sweden and Finland. These committees have already submitted their reports - in the spring and summer of 1991. The main ele ments of the proposed legislation in these three Nordic countries are the same. According to the Comjmittee, contemporary competition policy has little in common with Government efforts to ensure general price stability (as opposed to review of monopolies' rotes). Even ifdirect Government intervention in the form of price controls is not current poli cy, the possible future needfor such measures cannot be altogether excluded. Such measures may be necessary to prevent abnormal fluctu ations in the aggregate price level, due to ma jor national or international economic imba lances. But direct price intervention should always be weighted against alternative reme dies to ensure macroeconomic stability. The le gal authority to activate price controls does not fit easily into the Competition Act. Accor dingly, the Committee proposes a special Ge neral Price Measures Act vesting authority to establish price measures with the Government ifthere is a risk of such extraordinary price le vel fluctuations. The proposed Special Act in cludes provisions to implement both price con trols and notification procedures on price al terations. The legal authority is vested with the King in Council (i.e. the full council of mi nisters). If the measures are intended to last longer thanfour weeks, an affirmative vote in the Parliament will be required. Apart from establishing the necessary legal procedures, the Committee's report does not expound on the circumstances which might justify such exceptional measures.

in the Parliament will be required. Apart from establishing the necessary legal procedures, the Committee's report does not expound on the circumstances which might justify such exceptional measures.
However, it is demon strated how any direct regulation of prices adversely affects the level and pressure of com petition in the regulated markets - both when in force and after the regulation is abolished.

side 26

The proposed scope of the Competition Act is to reach all trades, regardless of whether the enterprise belongs in the private sector or is held by the Government, and regardless of whether any particular line of business also falls under special legislation. The sole propo sed general exception comprises labour tariffs and employment contracts. The wide scope suggested is essential if the statute is to be in strumental in promoting overall economic ef ficiency. These recommendations are in accor dance with OECD advice to member states, to the effect that particular sectors of the econo my should not be excluded from scrutiny un der general competition laws. As regards the geographical scope ofjuris diction, the Committee suggests that the statu te reaches all actions and agreements entered into in or de facto affecting Norway. However, actions and agreements purely affecting ex port markets, will be excluded unless the Go vernment otherwise decides. This suggested employment of the so called «Effects doctrine" as part of national competition law, brings Norway into line with dominant f oreignjuris dictions in thisfield. The Committee has given dose attention to the choice of a proper model for regulation - i.e. designing the right kind of competition statute. Technically, the proposal isfashioned as a mix - of flat prohibitions (per se rules) outlawing those business practices that from theoretical analysis as well as from practical experience are determined to be especially harmful; - and of provisions vesting legal au thority with an administrative agency to in tervene upon individual scrutiny against otherforms of harmful business practice. The Committee proposes three separate pro hibitions outlawing agreements among com petitors - i.e. in the horizontal plane. These are bans against price fixing, market sharing and any form of bid rigging. The proposed bans are to reach any kind ofconcerted action - express agreements as well as tacit collusion, and any understanding regardless of whether it is meant to be legally binding or merely in formally suggestive to the parties themselves. The ban against price fixing is to reach all kinds of prices - regardless of the term applied - as well as other payment components, inclu ding mark-up and discounts. Moreover, this ban comprises both agreements fixing exact prices and guidelines on calculation. The Committee proposes only one statutory prohibition against distributors' business practices - outlawing minimum retail prices.

both agreements fixing exact prices and guidelines on calculation. The Committee proposes only one statutory prohibition against distributors' business practices - outlawing minimum retail prices.
The ban against resale price maintenance re fers both tofixed prices and guidelines on cal culation, including guidance on mark-up and discounts. But the distributor will be allowed to fix maximum prices, and to recommend specific prices, as long as such recommenda tion only directs the retailer's final price and not the various components or the method of calculation. In order to make clear in the Competition Act itselfthat the proposed bans are not inten ded to excludeforms of cooperation that tradi tionally benefit rather than restrict competi tion, the most important exemptions are de tailed in the statute itself. Firstly, the prohibitions against horizontal understandings are not meant to prevent coo peration among enterprises which in any case may only influence the competitive situation to a limited extent. The introduction of a de minimis exemption is justified by theory as well as practical experience, evincing that co operation among several smaller firms may increase rather than decrease the competitive pressure in a particular market. Since Nor way is itself a small market with relatively few and large distributors in many sectors the de minimis limit is set at twenty percent joint market share. Even if twenty percent is a rela tively high share of any market, there is per ceived to be a certain need for cooperation in order to create countervailing power vis-a-vis established entities. In choosing a relatively ample volume exemption, the Committee also notes that the need for further exemptions in the statute itself, determined e.g. by participa ting firms' size (small and medium sized busi nesses), or the effects of particular business concepts (groups, chains orfranchising) is eli minated. Secondly, the Committee proposes on ex emption for licensing agreements, where the license refers to a registered patent or com mercial pattern. This exemption will only re ach cooperation between the licensor and the licensee. It is justified by the f act that the pro hibition against market sharing might other wise hamper dynamic efficency to the detri ment of the public good. Thirdly, the Committee proposes an exemp tion for joint venture cooperation on particu lar projects, provided that the purchaser in advance explicitly and in writing consents to the cooperation. Judging from experience, the ability to organize such ad hoc cartels often increases rather than decreases the competiti ve pressure, because smaller firms, or firms with complementing strength, may compete for assignments otherwise beyond their reach.

ad hoc cartels often increases rather than decreases the competiti ve pressure, because smaller firms, or firms with complementing strength, may compete for assignments otherwise beyond their reach.
This form of cooperation is most often used in contracting and construction, where formal bid rounds are put to service. But the Commit tee notes that a similar effect may be attained

side 27

in other lines of business - e.g. pooling insu rance risks, or syndicating loans. For this rea son, the proposed exemption is not limited to formal bids or to particular lines of business. By requiring express advance clearance from the purchaser in advance, the necessary safe guards should be in place. This requirement will also prevent the statutory joint venture exemption f rom legalizing continuing collusi ve efforts. Fourthly, the Committee submits that coope ration between a company and its owner, or between various companies in a concern, should be excluded from the prohibitions against both horizontal agreements and retail price maintenance. The general public may never plausibly expect competition between different entities within the same business structure to produce consumer surplus. Ifsuch entities compete, the extent of competition will always be subordinated to the owner's overri ding desire to reap the maximum profit flo wing from the combined enterprises' market power. Finally, the Committee proposes an exemp tion from the prohibition against pricefixing for cash discounts offered to business custo mers, limited to three percent on the sale price. Such cash discounts are often employed as standard terms of payment in Norway, as an alternative to credit periods. Since this prac tice cannot be shown to have had any adverse effects, it should not be banned. However, it must be noted that this exemption does not ex tend to discounts offered to consumers. Worka ble price competition for consumer business often takes the form of «discount wars». In addition to the statutory exemptions, the proposal contains a provision to except indi vidual agreements or generic forms of busi ness practice (so called «group exemptions») by administrative decree. The terms are that such agreement or practise boosts rather than restrict competition, or that other efficiency gains may flow from the venture. These terms are more or less similar to the requirementsfor exemption under EC competition rules. In ad dition, the Committee proposes as a narrowly defined exclusion criterion that «special con siderations» are demonstrated. This criterion is not fashioned to exclude entire trades, groups or sectors. Any such wider exceptions shall require special legislation under the comprehensive system proposed.

are demonstrated. This criterion is not fashioned to exclude entire trades, groups or sectors. Any such wider exceptions shall require special legislation under the comprehensive system proposed.
Because of the limited scope of the bans, the Committee proposes that the Competition Act also contain two specific provisions on the authority to intervene vis-a-vis otherwise le gal business practices, when such practises are deemed to contravene the regulatory pur pose ofeconomic efficiency. Firstly, the Committee suggests a provision with a general scope, enabling the authorities to ban or direct any business practice. How ever, the authorities may only intervene when satisfied that such practice unduly restricts competition contrary to the public interest. Secondly, the Committee submits that the Competition Act should empower the competi tion authorities to stop or direct mergers, when a merger is deemed to have materially adverse effects on the competition contrary to the public interest. Since mergers are more li kely than most business practises to produce efficiency gains, the terms of intervention are more restrictive vis-a-vis mergers. Moreover, the Committee suggests a system whereby the merging companies may notify the competi tion authorities to obtain their view on the ef fects of pending mergers. Such notification may be filed when a final agreement on the merger is in place. If the authorities subsequ ently take no action within three months upon receipt of such notification, they will be pre ventedfrom intervening. Moreover, regardless of whether the merging companies notify or not, the authorities are under a six months de adline to act against any merger. This deadli ne may be extended to one year under special circumstances (e.g. upon request from the companies in question). The merger control provision shall not only reach statutory mer gers, but any acquisition of a business enter prise. Upon its review of the restrictive business practices outlined above, the Committee emp hasizes the importance of extending the Com petition Act to other areas in order to promote the regulatory purpose ofeconomic efficiency: The Committee pays particularly attention to the importance of promoting market trans parency. In order to reduce consumer search costs, it is suggested that all vendors give noti ce of the prices charged to consumers - either in the form of price tags or by way of price lists or prominent displays. Moreover, it is proposed that the authorities be given the right to direct businesses to undertake other measures in order tofacilitate customers' revi ew of price and quality. Under the current law such directions have been given only rarely, but the authority to intervene should be pre served.

other measures in order tofacilitate customers' revi ew of price and quality. Under the current law such directions have been given only rarely, but the authority to intervene should be pre served.
Under the proposal, such authority will not be restricted to intervention infavour of consumers. The Committee stresses that an active infor mation policy, as well as the media attention paid to individual cases, are integral ele ments of a modem competition policy. Gene ral administrative procedure and freedom of information legislation applies to the compe tition enforcement. But the Committee assuside 28

mes that the competition authorities will also maintain an active policy on public informa tion, including disclosure of facts to the media and the general public to a wider extent thar: mandated under these statutes. However, the Committee also underscores that due attention should be given to the integ rity of physical persons involved - especially when a criminal investigation is pending. With particular regard to the importance of making collusive anti-competitive agree ments and practises publicly known so that customers may take countervailing action, the Committee suggests a provision authorizing the competition authorities to disclose the facts on any term or agreement among busi ness enterprises that may adversely effect competition. When deciding whether to disclo se or not, due regard should be given to the bu siness interest in keeping trade secrets. From its analysis of restrictive practices operated by the business enterprises themsel ves, the Committee turns to the competitive ef fects of various government regulations. The Committee stresses the importance of an acti ve competition advocacy program within the administration itself As a rule, government regulations influence competition in all regu lated markets. Accordingly, it is suggested that all proposals for new regulations with material competition effects be presented to the competition authorities for review before enactment. Correspondingly, a special provi sion is included in the Competition Act obli ging the competition authorities to raise the issue of anti-competitive effects of existing re gulations. lf the competition authorities find such anti-competitive effects to lack due rea son, notification shall be given to the ministry responsiblefor competition policy, so that the conflict may be resolved on a political level within the Government itself. The constant supervision and enforcement shall require an administrative apparatus as part of the Government. The Committee pro poses that the administrative responsibilities under the Competition Act be split between two levels of government. The mandate to pro pose legislation as well as regulations under the Act, and to set the priorities under current competition policy and propose allocation of resources in the government budget, is assig ned to the King and will probably be delega ted to one of the Government ministries.

priorities under current competition policy and propose allocation of resources in the government budget, is assig ned to the King and will probably be delega ted to one of the Government ministries.
The ongoing supervision of the various markets, investigations of and responses to individual violations, as well as the authority to interve ne against specific anti-competitive business practices, is assigned to an administrative agency. A majority of the Committee holds that the agency should be governed by a board of five members, and a competition director responsiblefor current affairs as well as wiel ding authority entrusted to him by the board. A minority of the Committee holds that the agency should be led solely by the director. The Committee proposes that the new agency be named The Bureau of Competition Supervi sion. The Committee does not detail thefuture or ganization chart of the Bureau. However, it is noted that the Bureau shall need a central unit capable of handling complex and taxing investigations, alongside continuous surveil lance of current developments. A majority of the Committee holds that there is no need for district offices as part of the Bureau. This ma jority presumes that major anti-competitive violations of the substantive rules laid down in the Ad, as well as anti-competitive business practices calling for intervention, will eventu ally reach the attention of the Bureau through complaints from consumers and competitors, and by way of media attention. The majority also emphasizes the importance of commissio ning the Bureau exclusively with competition enforcement. A minority of the Committee is of the opinion that the current system with dis trict offices could be handily transformed to benefit enforcement of the Competition Act. The minority also notes that the district offi ces, as under the current regime, should be able to handle other tasks - e.g. enforcement of possible price or wage controls. The minority concurs with respect to the necessity for a re sourceful central unit to supervise markets and enforce the various provisions in the Com petition Act. Administrative decisions by the competi tion authorities may radically affect their subjects, by altering their legal positions and methods of business. For this reason, the Com mittee stresses the importance of observing due process of law, as well as ensuring that private parties be secured substantive rights to protect their interests in the face of an inves tigation. It is submitted that all decisions by the Bureau of Competition Supervision may be appealed to a Competition Appeals Board. The Board members should be recruited among qualified lawyers and economists.

The Committee furthermore proposes that individual decisions under the Act should be enforceable under threat of an accumulating fine. if distribution costs decrea se, technology changes, deregulation takes place etc. In order to bolster the opportunity for busi ness enterprises to predetermine their legal position under the Competition Act, the Com mittee proposes that the Bureau may at their own choosing give advance notice or promise on the contents of individual decisions. Sepa rate notification procedures are also provided under the merger control provisions, and to clarify the Bureau's stance on the application of the de minimis exemption. The Committee advises that breaches of sta tutory provisions or of decisions under the Act should be criminal violations. Physical per sons may be punished with fines or imprison ment. Business entities could be punished with fines and loss of trading privileges. It is submitted that a criminal case may not be in stigated by public prosecutors unless the Bu reau of Competition Supervision has so direc ted. The object ofthis qualification is to make certain that criminal sanctions are only brought to bear in material cases. In addition to criminal sanctions, the Com mittee suggests a set ofsanctions in the form of forced divestiture offinancial benefits accru ed by way of transgression. This system of di vestiture is to be a purely civil remedy. In the case of a breach, the higher amount of the pro fit realized or 10 % of the business enterprise 's turnover in the market affected by the viola tion, may be divested in favour of the Govern ment treasury. The proposal is influenced by the EC's system of economic sanctions under Community competition rules. In determi ning the amount of divestiture due regard should be given to the severity and duration of the transgression, the potential for public harm, as well as the profit realized or expec ted. The Bureau of Competition Supervision will be empowered to present a motion for an out-of-court settlement to the alleged offender. But ifsuch proposal is turned down, any peti tion for divestiture shall be iransferred to the courts for civil litigation. However, if crimi nal charges are brought simultaneously, di vestiture proceedings are to be included in the criminal case. The Committee refrains from suggesting that the current system for resolution of priva te disputes by an administrative body be pro longed. Dispute resolution should as a general rule not be mixed with enforcement efforts un der the Competition Act warranted by the pu blic interest in functioning markets.

But the Committee stresses that the Competition Act is also intended to protect the interests of private parties, and that the various rules may be in voked in civil proceedings before the courts - on i.a. the right to delivery, compensationsfor losses incurred, as well as requests for tempo rary injunctions when such ciaims are made.

side 30

The Committee accordingly suggests some reforms in order tofacilitate the use of the ge neral courts. Firstly, it is to be illegal to refuse delivery, if such refusal will contravene the substantive rules of the Competition Act, or of administrative decisions under the Act. Se condly, any contract violating the substantive rules of the Act shall be null and void, but only so far as such contract is in contravention of the Act, unless it will be unconscionable to in voke the rest of the contract 's terms. Finally, it is suggested that the Bureau of Competition Supervision may intervene with a directive compelling a business entity to do business with other parties, provided that such a meas ure is a necessary element in the enforcement of the public interest in functioning markets. The Committee's proposals are intended to replace the 1953 Act on Control ofPrices, Pro fits and Restraints of Competition, as well as enforcement rules in a special Actfrom 1948, and substantive rules on resale price mainte nance in a regulation of 1957, and on price fixing and bid rigging in a regulation of 1960. The 1953 Act also contains various other pro visions deemed to be outdated, which the Com mittee accordingly suggests be abolished. Finally, the Committee has included a pro vision in the Competition Act facilitating as sistance to foreign or supranational competi tion authorities. The proposal covers the EC Commission's requirements on assistance from EC member states under Community law. As such, the proposal will cover any simi lar requirement on the enforcement of supra national competition rules in a potential Eu ropean Economic Area treaty. Negotiations on such a treaty are currently pending betwe en the EC and the European Free Trade Asso ciation member states.
